abstract: ArXiv:2609.01748v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study minimal residual space-time finite element discretizations of linear parabolic initial value problems in canonical space-time variational form. To deal with the arising dual norm, we introduce the Riesz lift of the residual as an additional variable. Quasi-optimality of the primal variable of the mixed system follows from a uniform inf-sup condition. This condition is known to be satisfied for finite element spaces w.r.t. prismatic partitions of the space-time cylinder that allow for a decomposition into time-slabs. We prove that this condition cannot be expected to hold otherwise. To recover stability for general partitions and the data at hand, we derive an a posteriori condition on the error between the exact Riesz lift of the residual and its Galerkin approximation -- being the secondary variable of our system -- under which the primal variable is quasi-optimal. We derive a posteriori error estimators for both variables, and use them in a double-adaptive loop that alternates test-space with trial-space enrichment. We illustrate our findings with numerical experiments in [MATH] and [MATH] dimensions.
tldr: This paper presents a double-adaptive solver for parabolic PDEs using space-time finite element methods with a posteriori error control.
motivation: To achieve efficient and accurate numerical solutions of parabolic initial value problems, the authors aim to develop an adaptive method that refines both time and space discretizations.
method: The method uses minimal residual space-time FEM, introduces a Riesz lift of the residual as an extra variable, derives an inf-sup condition, and employs a posteriori error estimators in a double-adaptive loop that alternates test-space and trial-space enrichment.
result: The paper proves that quasi-optimality of the primal variable holds under a derived a posteriori condition and includes numerical experiments in 2D and 3D illustrating the method's performance.
conclusion: The proposed double-adaptive solver is effective for parabolic problems, but the work is purely numerical mathematics and unrelated to quantum information or other specified research directions.

title: CRB-Guided Sensing And Resource Allocation For Human Pose Prediction In Integrated Sensing, Communication, And Computation Systems
authors: Zhonghao Liu, Yahao Ding, Jiaxiang Wang, Zhaohui Yang, Abdol Hamid Aghvami, Mohammad Shikh-Bahaei
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01908v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrated sensing, communication, and computation (ISCC) provides a promising framework for indoor human-centric applications. In these applications, short-term human pose prediction facilitates continuous human pose tracking and proactive resource allocation. This paper proposes a Cramer-Rao bound (CRB)-guided sensing framework and investigates a problem of minimizing prediction error in resource-constrained ISCC systems. Specifically, a pose prediction model (ET-Mamba) is first developed to predict human joint positions for continuous tracking. To account for computation-resource limitations, lightweight prediction heads are attached to different inference layers, enabling adaptive-depth pose prediction. A CRB-guided perturbation strategy is then introduced to translate sensing uncertainty at different sensing SNR levels into point-cloud perturbations. Based on that, an empirical relationship among pose prediction error, sensing SNR, and model inference depth is established. Furthermore, to improve prediction accuracy under limited resources, this paper formulates a resource allocation optimization problem that minimizes the pose prediction error by jointly optimizing the beamforming matrix, model inference depth, and computation frequency. To solve this mixed-integer non-convex optimization problem, we propose an alternating optimization (AO)-based algorithm, where closed-form updates and semidefinite programming (SDP) are integrated into the iterative solution process. Simulation results show that the proposed method effectively improves pose prediction performance by up to 35 percent under resource constraints, verifying the effectiveness of conducting joint sensing, communication, and computation design in ISCC systems.
tldr: This paper proposes a CRB-guided sensing and resource allocation framework for human pose prediction in integrated sensing, communication, and computation (ISCC) systems, achieving up to 35% improvement in prediction performance under resource constraints.
motivation: To enable continuous human pose tracking and proactive resource allocation in indoor human-centric applications, addressing computation and sensing resource limitations in ISCC systems.
method: Develops a lightweight ET-Mamba pose prediction model with adaptive-depth inference, introduces a CRB-guided perturbation strategy to model sensing uncertainty, and formulates a mixed-integer non-convex resource allocation optimization problem solved via alternating optimization with closed-form updates and semidefinite programming.
result: Simulations demonstrate that the proposed method improves pose prediction accuracy by up to 35% under resource constraints, validating the effectiveness of joint sensing, communication, and computation design.
conclusion: The paper confirms that integrating sensing, communication, and computation design enhances performance in ISCC systems, providing a foundation for future resource allocation strategies in similar human-centric applications.

title: Two Adjoint Perspectives On Fokker-Planck Optimization: A Microscopic-Macroscopic Correspondence
authors: Kathrin Hellmuth, Qin Li, Yunan Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02072v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Fokker-Planck equation admits both a macroscopic Eulerian description through probability densities and a microscopic Lagrangian description through stochastic trajectories. Consequently, optimization problems constrained by the Fokker-Planck equation can be formulated from either perspective. Surprisingly, the corresponding adjoint equations appear to be fundamentally different: the macroscopic adjoint is governed by the backward Kolmogorov equation, whereas the microscopic adjoint evolves pathwise along stochastic trajectories. In this note, we reconcile these two formulations by establishing their correspondence in the continuum setting. We further show that, although their discrete gradients no longer coincide after discretization, both provide consistent numerical approximations of the continuum gradient. Explicit convergence rates are established for both discretization strategies.
tldr: This paper reconciles the macroscopic and microscopic adjoint formulations for Fokker-Planck optimization, proving their continuum equivalence and analyzing discrete approximations.
motivation: The authors noticed that adjoint equations derived from macroscopic (density) and microscopic (trajectory) perspectives appear different, so they aimed to reconcile these approaches.
method: They derive the adjoint equations from both perspectives, establish their correspondence in the continuum, and then analyze discretized gradient computations, providing convergence rates.
result: The two formulations are shown to be equivalent in the continuum; after discretization, both yield consistent approximations with explicit convergence rates.
conclusion: The study provides a unified theoretical framework linking two practical adjoint approaches for Fokker-Planck constrained optimization, validating their numerical consistency.

title: Constraint-Preserving Genetic Algorithms For Embedding Linear Codes Into Self-Orthogonal Codes
authors: Haeun Lim, Junmin An, Jon-Lark Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02135v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we aim to construct binary optimal self-orthogonal codes using shortest self-orthogonal embedding methods. For this purpose, we design a heuristic framework based on a genetic algorithm. We explore the search space of shortest self-orthogonal embeddings using a fitness function based on the minimum distance and the number of minimum-weight codewords. We construct crossover and mutation operations so that every chromosome yields a valid self-orthogonal embedding, while high-fitness structural features, such as favorable subsequences of orthogonal generators, are propagated across generations. We also analyze the time and storage complexity of the algorithm, and validate our design through an ablation study on guided crossover and a comparison with random search under an equal time budget. Using this method, we obtain [MATH] new binary optimal self-orthogonal codes that meet the upper bound, together with [MATH] further self-orthogonal codes attaining the best minimum distance found so far.
tldr: Proposes a constraint-preserving genetic algorithm to embed binary linear codes into self-orthogonal codes, yielding many new optimal codes.
motivation: To efficiently construct binary optimal self-orthogonal codes using shortest self-orthogonal embedding methods.
method: Uses a genetic algorithm with tailored crossover and mutation operations that ensure every chromosome yields a valid self-orthogonal embedding, guided by a fitness function based on minimum distance and number of minimum-weight codewords.
result: Obtained new binary optimal self-orthogonal codes that meet the upper bounds, and additional codes attaining the best minimum distance found so far.
conclusion: The genetic algorithm is effective and validated via ablation studies and comparison with random search.

title: The Tensor Category For W(2,2)-vertex Algebra
authors: Drazen Adamovic, Mingjie Peng, Gordan Radobolja, Jinwei Yang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02202v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies the category [MATH] of grading-restricted [MATH]-cofinite generalized modules for the vertex operator algebra associated to the [MATH]-algebra [MATH]. We first show that [MATH] is the same as the category of finite length modules whose simple composition factors are the irreducible highest weight [MATH]--modules [MATH] of highest weight [MATH] for [MATH], and hence [MATH] carries a braided tensor category structure. Then we prove the fusion rules for the simple objects [MATH] are governed by the [MATH] Clebsch--Gordan rule. In particular, we prove \[ L[r]\boxtimes L[s]\cong \bigoplus_{i=0}^{\min\{r,s\}-1} L[r+s-1-2i]. \] Using the fusion rules and a recent result of Etingof--Penneys, we establish the rigidity of [MATH]. We also show the semisimple subcategory generated by the simple objects [MATH] is tensor equivalent to the category Rep [MATH] of finite dimensional [MATH]-modules.
tldr: This paper studies the braided tensor category of modules for the W(2,2) vertex algebra, proving fusion rules and rigidity.
motivation: To understand the structure of modules for W(2,2)-algebras, which are important in conformal field theory and vertex operator algebra theory.
method: They show that the category of grading-restricted, C1-cofinite generalized modules is equivalent to finite length modules with certain irreducibles, derive fusion rules using Clebsch-Gordan, and use recent result by Etingof-Penneys to establish rigidity.
result: They prove the fusion rules for simple objects follow the Clebsch-Gordan rule, and establish the rigidity of the category. Additionally, they show that a semisimple subcategory is tensor equivalent to the category of finite-dimensional modules for a certain group.
conclusion: The work provides a rigorous tensor category structure for W(2,2) modules, contributing to the mathematical theory of vertex algebras and their representations.

title: Agentic UE-CoMIMO For 6g Terminals: From Virtual Antenna Augmentation To AI-Native Virtualization
authors: Chao-Kai Wen, Yen-Cheng Chan, Lung-Sheng Tsai, Pei-Kai Liao, Geoffrey Ye Li
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02290v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: End-user-centric collaborative MIMO (UE-CoMIMO) lets nearby devices form a virtual multi-antenna terminal to overcome the antenna limitations of individual user equipment. Extending such cooperation to communication, sensing, computing, and task-relevant information exchange requires a control layer that can interpret user intent, select cooperation mechanisms, and replan as conditions change. This article introduces Agentic UE-CoMIMO, in which device micro-agents, a smartphone or CPE hub agent, and edge/network agents coordinate device participation, relay modes, traffic splitting and duplication, compute placement, semantic-token exchange, and topology reconfiguration. Two system-level scenario studies on creator-centric live streaming and wearable-collaborative blind-spot sensing compare the proposed controller with capability-matched adaptive baselines. The results show that, by anticipating changes and preparing cooperation and fallback actions in advance, agentic control sustains high-quality streaming for longer and maintains blind-spot warnings through device outages. We also discuss the associated standardization, interoperability, trust, and validation challenges.
tldr: The paper presents Agentic UE-CoMIMO, an AI-native multi-agent framework for collaborative MIMO in 6G terminals, coordinating communication, sensing, computing, and semantic exchange among devices.
motivation: To overcome individual antenna limitations and enable end-user-centric cooperation in 6G, requiring a control layer to interpret user intent and dynamically manage device collaboration and reconfiguration.
method: The approach uses device micro-agents, a hub agent, and edge/network agents to control participation, relay modes, traffic flows, compute placement, and topology, evaluated via two system-level scenario studies with capability-matched baselines.
result: Agentic control sustains high-quality streaming for longer durations and maintains blind-spot warnings through device outages, outperforming adaptive baselines by anticipating changes and preparing fallback actions.
conclusion: Agentic collaboration enhances reliability and efficiency for 6G terminal cooperation, but faces challenges in standardization, interoperability, trust, and validation.

title: A Simple Derivation Of The Kalman Filter
authors: Marco Chiani, Giovanni Petris, Moe Z. Win
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02332v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this lecture note, we present a concise and self-contained derivation of the discrete-time Kalman filter equations that requires only a basic understanding of least squares estimation. The treatment is designed to minimize mathematical overhead while preserving both rigor and generality.
tldr: A concise lecture note providing a simple derivation of the discrete-time Kalman filter using only basic least squares estimation.
motivation: To present the Kalman filter derivation in an accessible manner with minimal mathematical overhead, suitable for educational purposes.
method: The derivation leverages least squares estimation principles and is presented in a self-contained, concise format.
result: A rigorous and general derivation of the Kalman filter equations without requiring advanced stochastic calculus.
conclusion: The paper serves as a useful pedagogical resource for understanding the Kalman filter, but does not contribute to the specified research directions in quantum information or related fields.

title: The Knot Invariant Associated To Two-Parameter Quantum Algebras Ii
authors: Tianhao Zhu Zhaobing Fan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02481v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fan, Ma, and Xing constructed oriented-tangle invariants from finite-type two-parameter quantum algebras. In this paper, we construct an explicit parameter-transport comparison between two-parameter modules and their corresponding one-parameter modules, and we verify this comparison on every elementary oriented-tangle operator. After extending scalars to a common coefficient field, we prove that if [MATH] is any finite-dimensional integrable type-1 simple highest-weight [MATH]-module whose weights lie in an admissible lattice and [MATH] is its transported module, then for every oriented link [MATH], the corresponding normalized invariants satisfy [MATH]. Consequently, the two invariants assign equal values to exactly the same pairs of oriented links and therefore have the same distinguishing power; this includes the vector representations of the finite classical types A, B, C, and D. Sean Clark's comparison of ordinary and super quantum knot invariants is obtained as a specialization of the same transport principle in which explicit scalar factors are allowed.
tldr: This paper studies knot invariants from two-parameter quantum algebras and shows they coincide with one-parameter invariants via parameter transport, implying identical distinguishing power.
motivation: The authors aim to clarify the relationship between two-parameter and one-parameter quantum algebra invariants, extending prior work on oriented-tangle invariants.
method: They construct an explicit parameter-transport comparison between two-parameter modules and one-parameter modules, verify it on all elementary tangle operators, and prove equality of normalized invariants for finite-dimensional integrable type-1 simple highest-weight modules on an admissible lattice.
result: The invariants from two-parameter and one-parameter algebras assign equal values to the same pairs of oriented links, covering vector representations of finite classical types A, B, C, D, and specializing to Sean Clark's comparison.
conclusion: The two families of quantum invariants have the same distinguishing power, so two-parameter algebras do not provide stronger knot invariants in this setting.

title: Learning Parametric Monotone Games
authors: Tatiana Tatarenko Alberto Bemporad
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02494v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the problem of learning from data a parametric Nash equilibrium (NE) problem that is monotone (or strongly monotone) for all parameter values. In the presence of local and shared convex constraints, monotonicity enables efficient computation of generalized Nash equilibria of the learned game. We consider two learning scenarios: (i) direct learning of the NE problem from samples of the agents' costs, and (ii) inverse learning of surrogate agents' costs from samples of their best responses. We propose two methods to solve these tasks. The first is a penalty-based approach that promotes monotonicity of the learned game during training. The second, based on a representation theorem we introduce for a broad class of monotone games, parameterizes the agents' costs so that monotonicity of the NE problem is guaranteed by construction, for all parameter values, regardless of the training data used. We illustrate the applicability of the proposed methods on several numerical examples. A Python library and the examples reported in the paper are available at [URL].
tldr: This paper studies learning parametric monotone games from data, proposing methods to learn cost functions that guarantee monotonicity for all parameter values.
motivation: Efficient computation of generalized Nash equilibria relies on monotonicity, and learning such games from data is underexplored.
method: A penalty-based approach promotes monotonicity during training, and a representation theorem allows parameterization that guarantees monotonicity by construction.
result: Numerical examples show the applicability of both methods for learning monotone Nash equilibrium problems.
conclusion: The proposed methods enable data-driven learning of monotone parametric games while preserving structural properties for equilibrium computation.

title: Projected Subgradient Methods For A Class Of Nonsmooth And Nonconvex Optimization Problems
authors: Christian Kanzow, Jannis Kr\"uger, Leo Lehmann
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02517v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate the optimization problem of minimizing a nonsmooth function that satisfies a nonsmooth version of the descent lemma over a nonempty and closed but not necessarily convex set. The objective function belongs to the class of upper-[MATH] functions, whereas the constraints may promote a sparse or low-rank structure. We propose a projected subgradient method with two different globalization strategies: (a) a nonmonotone linesearch and, under additional assumptions, (b) an auto-conditioned method, where the stepsize is given by a formula depending on data from past iterations. We show that both methods converge to solutions that satisfy a stronger stationarity concept than one would expect from the subdifferential sum-rule, which is particularly important since the optimization problems of interest are inherently nonconvex. Finally, we present promising numerical results when applying the algorithm to an MPEC-style problem as well as the matrix optimization problems MAXCUT and Robust PCA.
tldr: This paper introduces projected subgradient methods with globalization strategies for nonsmooth nonconvex optimization, demonstrating convergence to strong stationarity and promising numerical results on MPEC, MAXCUT, and Robust PCA.
motivation: To tackle optimization problems with nonsmooth objectives and nonconvex constraints, which often arise in sparse/low-rank matrix problems, and to develop efficient algorithms with convergence guarantees.
method: The authors propose two projected subgradient methods, one using nonmonotone linesearch and one auto-conditioned, ensuring convergence to a stronger stationarity concept without requiring convexity.
result: The algorithms show strong convergence properties and perform well numerically on problems like MAXCUT and Robust PCA.
conclusion: The methods extend projected subgradient techniques to a broader class of nonsmooth nonconvex problems, offering practical algorithms with theoretical backing.

title: Skill-as-API: Confidential Multi-Agent Coordination For Agentic Software Engineering
authors: Ziwei Zhao, Yu Gu, Haojun Liang, Chen Zhang, Xizhi Ding
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01677v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI coding agents are evolving from solitary tools into collaborative teammates that discover and invoke one another's specialized skills. But the coordination channel itself can leak a skill's intellectual property. Protocols such as MCP and A2A run implementations server-side, yet they still publish each skill's description and typed schemas to every peer, offer no way to hide a skill's existence, and cannot guarantee that a wrapped system prompt stays off the wire. Application-layer privacy filters help, but act only after the model has decided to emit sensitive text. We take a complementary, protocol-layer route: Skill-as-API, a coordination protocol whose public view of a skill is limited to its name, description, typed input/output schemas, and trust tier. The skill body is closure-captured in the owner's process and never crosses the wire. Four layers add access control and narrow the prompt-injection surface structurally rather than by filtering content. We provide an open-source Python implementation over XMTP with 1.8-2.9 s cross-continent hot-reconnect latency, and a software-engineering case study in which three agents coordinate a pull-request review while each retains ownership of its proprietary analysis prompts.
tldr: Proposes Skill-as-API, a protocol-layer approach to protect the intellectual property of AI agent skills during multi-agent coordination.
motivation: Existing coordination protocols like MCP and A2A expose skill descriptions and schemas, risking leakage of proprietary methods. Application-level filters are insufficient, so a structural solution is needed.
method: Skill-as-API limits public view to name, description, schemas, and trust tier, while closure-capturing skill bodies in the owner's process. Four layers of access control and structural prompt-injection mitigation are implemented.
result: An open-source Python implementation over XMTP achieves 1.8-2.9 s cross-continent hot-reconnect latency, demonstrated in a case study where three agents coordinate a pull-request review while retaining proprietary analysis prompts.
conclusion: The protocol successfully preserves skill confidentiality in multi-agent coordination, offering a structural alternative to content filtering.

title: Agent Memory Is A Surface For Endogenous Authorization Laundering
authors: Tommaso Cerruti, Mika Okamoto, Ansel Kaplan Erol
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01836v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Long-running LLM agents rely on persistent memory to carry state across interactions, including permissions, restrictions, and revocations. When memory misrepresents this evolving authorization state, the agent's own records can grant authority that the underlying history never permitted, resulting in misaligned behavior without any external attacks. We term this failure endogenous authorization laundering, where spurious permissions written into memory lead to unauthorized actions as their provenance is washed away. We then introduce EAL-Bench, which measures how accurately persistent memory preserves evolving authorization state and whether errors propagate to downstream unauthorized actions. We evaluate five LLMs as memory writers and two as executors across procurement, cybersecurity, and finance. We find that under incremental memory updates, writers create false authority for up to 50.2% of unauthorized requests; once false authority is present, executors act on it in 98.6% of trials. Two safeguards, requiring stored permissions to be backed by valid source events, and tracking permission changes through bounded event sourcing, substantially reduce laundering, but both also reject more legitimate actions, exposing a safety-utility tradeoff. Persistent memory is therefore not merely a performance component, but a part of an LLM agent's effective authorization policy.
tldr: The paper identifies a failure mode in LLM agents where persistent memory can misrepresent authorization state, leading to unauthorized actions without external attacks.
motivation: Long-running LLM agents rely on memory to carry permissions, but memory can erroneously grant authority, causing misaligned behavior.
method: Introduces EAL-Bench, evaluates five LLMs as memory writers and two as executors, tests safeguards like event sourcing.
result: False authority generated up to 50.2% of unauthorized requests, and actions taken on it in 98.6% of trials; safeguards reduce but reject legitimate actions.
conclusion: Memory is part of authorization policy; needs safeguards.

title: C$^2$T-OpenMax: A Novel Open-Set WiFi Rf Fingerprinting Method Via Center Constrained Learning And Confidence-Guided Tail Modeling
authors: Yuanyu Zhang, Junjie Yang, Ji He, Shuangrui Zhao, Lele Zheng, Yulong Shen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02007v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Radio frequency fingerprinting (RFF) enables device authentication from transmitter-specific hardware imperfections, but practical deployment requires cross-environment open-set recognition. Data augmentation improves environmental generalization, yet may yield dispersed, low-confidence known-class representations that distort the class statistics used by OpenMax. To address this problem, we propose C[MATH]T-OpenMax, an enhanced OpenMax framework combining center-constrained learning with confidence-guided tail modeling. The former improves intra-class compactness, making class-wise representations more suitable for distance-based modeling. The latter retains only correctly classified, high-confidence logits for mean activation vector estimation and Weibull fitting, reducing bias from ambiguous boundary samples. Together, the two modules refine representation geometry and OpenMax construction while preserving augmentation benefits. Experiments on a public WiFi CSI dataset show that C[MATH]T-OpenMax achieves the highest open-set accuracy in seven of eight location groups and outperforms all baselines in area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and open-set classification rate (OSCR) across every tested openness level. Under the largest-openness setting, it improves accuracy by 12.31%, AUROC by 0.0887, and OSCR by 0.0856 over the augmented OpenMax baseline.
tldr: This paper proposes C^2T-OpenMax, an open-set WiFi radio frequency fingerprinting method using center-constrained learning and confidence-guided tail modeling, achieving improved cross-environment recognition accuracy.
motivation: Radio frequency fingerprinting requires cross-environment open-set recognition but data augmentation can distort class statistics used by OpenMax, reducing performance.
method: The method combines center-constrained learning to improve intra-class compactness and confidence-guided tail modeling to retain only correctly classified, high-confidence logits for better Weibull fitting.
result: Experiments on a public WiFi CSI dataset show the method achieves the highest open-set accuracy in most settings and outperforms baselines in AUROC and OSCR.
conclusion: The proposed enhancements refine representation geometry and OpenMax construction, preserving augmentation benefits and improving open-set recognition performance.

title: Agentic Settlement Protocol: An Application Profile For Refundable, Delayed-Fulfilment Agent Commerce On Stablecoin Rails
authors: Behnam (beny), Mohammadkhani, Atul Khekade, Ritesh Kakkad
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02208v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous agents can already pay per request: HTTP-native protocols such as x402 let an agent sign a stablecoin authorization and receive a resource in the same round trip. That model is atomic and final, which suits metered access and fails commerce: a purchase made on a person's behalf -- a service appointment, a physical order, a flight -- is large, frequently cancelled, and should not become the seller's money until delivery. We present the Agentic Settlement Protocol (ASP), an application profile over on-chain authorize-and-capture escrow (as standardised by the Commerce Payments Protocol) for businesses whose fulfilment is confirmed off-chain by their own order, scheduling, invoicing or booking system, abstracted as a fulfilment engine. ASP contributes: a three-deadline hold model separating the issuance deadline, escrow expiry and the engine's inventory expiry by an explicit submission-inclusion-finality margin, under which no inventory is issued against reclaimable funds; a fulfilment-verification ladder stating who is trusted to trigger capture, what their attestation proves, and under what challenge window; engine-authoritative partial refunds with a refund-liquidity order and per-seller exposure controls, including atomic exposure reservation, that bound the operator's credit risk; distributor revenue share that is provably unprofitable to self-deal; a single-currency-per-charge invariant; and a normative interface specification (x402 scheme, vault ABI, operator and connector APIs, conformance levels) intended to let independent implementations interoperate. The design originated in a review of travel-agency participation in agentic settlement and is instantiated on the XDC Network. This is a design paper; a fault-injection evaluation plan is specified and measurement is left to follow-up work.
tldr: The paper proposes the Agentic Settlement Protocol (ASP), an application profile for enabling refundable, delayed-fulfillment commerce by autonomous agents using stablecoin escrow and a three-deadline hold model.
motivation: Autonomous agents require a payment mechanism that suits large, cancellable purchases rather than atomic, final payments, which are inadequate for services like appointments or physical orders.
method: ASP defines an on-chain authorize-and-capture escrow model with three deadlines (issuance, escrow expiry, inventory expiry) to prevent inventory release against reclaimable funds, a fulfillment-verification ladder for trust management, engine-authoritative partial refunds, exposure controls, distributor revenue share, and a single-currency invariant, along with normative interfaces.
result: The paper provides a detailed design specification and normative interface (x402 scheme, vault ABI, operator/connector APIs) instantiated on the XDC Network, but intentionally omits empirical evaluation, leaving a fault-injection plan for future work.
conclusion: ASP aims to support a wide range of agent-based commerce with refunds and delayed fulfillment, but its practical efficacy remains to be demonstrated through follow-up fault-injection testing.

title: Polynomial Invariants For Probabilistic Transition Systems With Unbounded Support
authors: Anne Schreuder, Lorenz Winkler, Laura Kov\'acs, C. -H. Luke Ong
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02446v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the synthesis of polynomial invariants for probabilistic transition systems (PTS) based on martingale theory. We present tractable methods to verify that such polynomials are indeed invariants, in the sense that their expected value upon termination is the same as their value at the start of the computation. We do this by applying the Optional Stopping Theorem (OST) in the form of a specific precondition. This precondition requires the existence of an integrable dominating function for the martingale expression, which implies uniform integrability; we refer to this condition as dui. For linear PTS we simplify the dui property to proving finiteness of the expected value of an expression depending on the update matrix, the degree of the martingale expression, and the stopping time. Specifically, if all random samples have finite moments and we can verify a moment bound on the runtime of a linear loop, then we can automatically synthesise polynomial loop invariants that satisfy the OST. Notably, dui allows for the sampled distributions to have unbounded support, which is a novel contribution to the field.
tldr: This paper proposes methods to synthesize polynomial invariants for probabilistic transition systems with unbounded support using martingale theory and the Optional Stopping Theorem.
motivation: Verification of probabilistic programs often relies on invariants, but existing techniques are limited to distributions with bounded support, leaving a gap for unbounded cases.
method: The authors apply the Optional Stopping Theorem with a condition for uniform integrability (dui), and simplify it for linear probabilistic transition systems by checking finiteness of expected values.
result: They show that if random samples have finite moments and a moment bound on runtime holds, polynomial loop invariants satisfying the OST can be synthesized automatically.
conclusion: This work extends polynomial invariant synthesis to distributions with unbounded support, presenting a novel contribution to probabilistic program verification.

title: Spade: SPaT Attack Detection From The Connected Vehicle's Perspective
authors: James Di Novo, Hany Ragab, Sylvain P. Leblanc
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02741v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Signal Phase and Timing (SPaT) messages are a cornerstone of connected vehicle (CV) safety, enabling CVs to perceive and respond to intersection state through Vehicle-to-Infrastructure (V2I) and Vehicle-to-Vehicle (V2V) communication. The integrity of these messages is threatened by a range of application-layer attacks that can bypass conventional authentication when a roadside unit or peer vehicle is compromised. Existing intrusion detection research either defends the infrastructure side or targets V2V Basic Safety Message (BSM) / Cooperative Awareness Message (CAM) misbehavior, leaving the onboard CV perspective on SPaT integrity unaddressed.To close this gap, we introduce SPADE --- the SPaT Attack Detection and Evaluation dataset --- a labelled, multi-modal, simulation-based dataset designed specifically for deep learning IDS research in this space. SPADE is generated through Eclipse MOSAIC using runtime attack injection at the SAE J2735 application layer across six attack classes and one benign class. By combining four intersection geometries, six operating conditions, and five independent random-seed repetitions, SPADE comprises 180 unique base scenario runs, yielding [MATH]1,890,000 labelled timestep records (270,000 per class). Each record fuses SPaT message fields, onboard camera confidence scores, and cooperative V2V peer data across 40 features, reflecting the multi-modal signal space required to distinguish deliberate attacks from environmental degradation. The dataset, generation code, and scenario configurations are released publicly to support reproducible and comparative IDS research in C-V2X security. The developed toolbox, instructions, and dataset link are publicly available on GitHub: [URL].
tldr: This paper introduces SPADE, a simulated multisignal dataset for deep learning intrusion detection of SPaT message attacks from a connected vehicle's perspective.
motivation: Existing intrusion detection for connected vehicles targets infrastructure or basic safety messages, leaving the onboard vehicle side vulnerable to corrupted SPaT messages. This paper addresses that gap by providing a dataset for research.
method: The authors built the dataset using Eclipse MOSAIC, injecting six attack classes and one benign class at the SAE J2735 application layer across various intersection geometries and conditions. Each record combines SPaT fields, camera confidence, and V2V peer data into 40 features.
result: SPADE produces 1,890,000 labeled timestep records (270,000 per class) across 180 base scenarios, designed for deep learning IDS evaluation.
conclusion: The dataset and tools are released publicly to enable reproducible research in C-V2X security, specifically for SPaT integrity.

title: Quantum Circuit And Tensor Network Implementation Of The 2d Acoustic Wave Equation
authors: Gabor Vattay Tamas Nemeth
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01904v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a cohesive framework for simulating seismic wave propagation utilizing quantum computing paradigms and their classical tensor network equivalents. We detail a quantum circuit-based formulation for the explicit finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) solution of the two-dimensional acoustic wave equation and map this quantum architecture onto a tensor train representation, namely for Matrix Product State (MPS). The MPS solver enables deterministic simulation of large-scale wavefield dynamics on classical high-performance computing systems. We demonstrate the MPS representation by computing 2D seismic wavefields on the Marmousi model. Our results indicate that the MPS representation is a viable direction for computing and scaling wavefield propagation.
tldr: This paper presents a quantum circuit formulation for the 2D acoustic wave equation and maps it to a matrix product state (MPS) representation for classical simulation, demonstrating the approach on the Marmousi model.
motivation: To explore quantum computing paradigms for seismic wave simulation and provide a scalable classical alternative via tensor networks, aiming to handle large-scale wavefield dynamics.
method: The authors develop an explicit finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) solution as a quantum circuit, then transform this circuit into a matrix product state (MPS) tensor train format for efficient classical high-performance computing.
result: The MPS representation is successfully applied to simulate 2D seismic wavefields on the Marmousi model, indicating that this approach can scale wavefield propagation deterministically.
conclusion: The matrix product state representation is a viable direction for computational seismology, bridging quantum circuit models with classical tensor network solvers, though it does not align with the user's core research directions.

title: The Hessian Of Planar Central Configurations In Pair Space: Decomposition, Morse Index And Symmetry Reduction
authors: Manuele Santoprete
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01857v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give a variational derivation of the central configuration equations in pair space, where the relative position vectors between pairs of bodies serve as the primary variables. Vector Lagrange multipliers enforce the linear triangle relations required for these pair vectors to be realizable in the plane. For arbitrary [MATH], we show that the constrained Hessian decomposes as [MATH], where the gap Laplacian [MATH] is positive semidefinite and the transverse Laplacian [MATH] is signed and contains all possible negative directions. For non-collinear planar four-body central configurations, the signed part has rank two. This yields a new proof of the known bound that the Morse index is at most two. We then characterize positive definiteness and degeneracy of the Hessian by the eigenvalues of an explicit [MATH] matrix or, equivalently, by two generalized eigenvalues of a pencil of symmetric matrices. We illustrate the general criterion using the equal-mass square central configuration. For reflection-symmetric configurations, the generalized eigenvalue problem decomposes into two independent smaller problems. This reduction applies to kite and isosceles trapezoidal configurations. For the trapezoid, however, the reflection acts non-orthogonally on the pair coordinates, giving a different, non-orthogonal reduction. Applying the reflection-symmetry reduction to the rhombus family, we prove that the Hessian is positive definite modulo the rotational zero mode; equivalently, every rhombus central configuration is nondegenerate modulo rotations and has Morse index zero.
tldr: This paper studies the Hessian of central configurations in planar N-body problems, focusing on decomposition, Morse index, and symmetry reduction, which is unrelated to quantum information or its adjacent fields.
motivation: The research interests are in quantum information, information thermodynamics, quantum networks, and hybrid quantum systems, while this paper is purely in celestial mechanics and dynamical systems.
method: The paper uses variational methods and pair-space coordinates to decompose the constrained Hessian, analyzing its positive definiteness and degeneracy via eigenvalue problems.
result: It proves that the Morse index of non-collinear planar four-body central configurations is at most two, and applies symmetry reduction to show positive definiteness for certain symmetric configurations.
conclusion: The paper does not connect to quantum information theory or any of the specified research directions, so it falls outside the user's interests.

title: Type-Directed, Secure-by-Construction Enclave Partitioning For Llvm
authors: Wesley B. Nuzzo, Samuel Dodson, Benjamin Houle, Tarakaram Gollamudi, Anitha Gollamudi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02048v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs) provide hardware-supported isolation through enclaves that protect code and data independently of software abstractions. However, TEEs alone cannot enforce information-flow security. This problem is further aggravated in LLVM-like low-level languages that allow unrestricted pointer manipulation and unstructured control flow. Moreover, using TEEs effectively typically requires manually partitioning applications into enclave and non-enclave components, a process that is labor-intensive, error-prone, and lacks fine-grained control. We address these challenges with a three-step approach. First, we formalize SIR, an enclave-oblivious calculus based on LLVM IR, equipped with a novel permissive type system that enforces security against low-level attackers. To obtain meaningful guarantees, SIR combines information-flow control with security-aware coarse-grained memory safety. Second, we extend SIR to SIREN, an enclave-aware calculus that enforces noninterference against stronger attackers capable of observing arbitrary non-enclave memory. Third, we develop a type-driven, type-preserving compilation from SIR to SIREN that automatically produces secure enclave-aware programs, eliminating manual partitioning while providing fine-grained control over host-enclave boundaries. We implement and evaluate SPLITR on thirteen microbenchmarks and real-world workloads, including applications from SGXGauge, on Intel SGX hardware. SPLITR scales to OpenSSL (425,953 LLVM IR instructions) and supports multiple objectives that expose trade-offs among enclave TCB size, host-enclave transitions, and boundary data movement. For OpenSSL, optimizing for transitions reduces them from 393 to 187. Runtime overhead is dominated by fixed enclave costs for short-running workloads, whereas long-running applications better amortize these costs and approach native performance.
tldr: Presents a type-driven approach to automatically partition applications into enclave and non-enclave parts for trusted execution environments, combining information-flow control and memory safety.
motivation: TEEs alone cannot enforce information-flow security, and manually partitioning applications into enclave and non-enclave components is labor-intensive and error-prone.
method: Formalizes SIR, an enclave-oblivious calculus based on LLVM IR with a permissive type system, extends it to SIREN for enclave-aware security, and develops a type-preserving compilation from SIR to SIREN.
result: Implements and evaluates SPLITR on microbenchmarks and real workloads, scaling to OpenSSL and reducing enclave transitions from 393 to 187.
conclusion: The approach eliminates manual partitioning while providing fine-grained control over host-enclave boundaries, with runtime overhead dominated by fixed enclave costs.

title: Ranked By The Matcher: A Reproducibility Audit Of Knowledge Graph Extraction From Threat Reports
authors: Houbing Herbert Song Safayat Bin Hakim
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01671v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security teams and researchers choose knowledge-graph extraction tooling for threat reports on the strength of published triple-F1 scores, yet those scores depend on how predicted triples are matched to gold annotations. We could reimplement the stated matching rule for only five of twelve inspected systems. Re-scoring ten system outputs on shared documents under eight protocols reverses eleven of forty-five pairwise orderings; one fixed prediction set spans 0.16-0.70 F1. On GRID's external 378-item calibration set, no mechanical matcher (lexical, embedding, or entailment) agrees with multi-reviewer adjudication above 71%, whereas an LLM judge reaches 86%. To separate component effects from matcher rewards, we build CTIForge, whose deterministic validation layer can vary while extraction is held byte-identical. Across seven tested deployment configurations, validation raises precision for all four hosted backbones and lowers it for all three offline backbones. Because backbone, decoding, and backend-specific prompting covary, this is a descriptive split rather than an isolated serving effect. It coincides with a roughly 2.8-fold increase in actions explicitly disputing entity type, consistent with hand-written rules encoding the conventions of the extractor against which they were developed. We release the pipeline, protocol suite, and per-triple audit records.
tldr: This paper audits the reproducibility of knowledge graph extraction from threat reports, showing that reported scores heavily depend on the matching rule used, and proposes a controlled pipeline to isolate effects.
motivation: Security teams rely on triple-F1 scores to choose knowledge-graph extraction tools, but these scores may be unreliable due to inconsistent matching rules across systems.
method: The authors reimplement matching rules for five of twelve inspected systems, rescore outputs under eight protocols, and build CTIForge to separate validation effects while holding extraction fixed.
result: Matcher choice reverses eleven of forty-five pairings, no mechanical matcher beats 71% agreement with human adjudication, while an LLM judge reaches 86%, and validation layer effects vary by deployment.
conclusion: Evaluation of KG extraction is sensitive to matching rules, and the community needs standardized protocols, possibly leveraging LLM-based judging for more reliable assessments.

title: Inverse Planning Of Social Interactions In Relationships
authors: Alicia M. Chen, Ashley J. Thomas, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Rebecca Saxe
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a formal account of how structured, shared knowledge about social relationships shapes action interpretation. The model represents relationships as constraints in a social environment, analogous to boundaries or obstacles in a physical environment and operating within the same generative model, but exerting distinct constraints on action. As an initial test of this framework, we draw on research across the social sciences to capture in the models how one dimension of relationships -- formality versus intimacy -- shapes how people interpret interpersonally vulnerable behavior. We test this account in stories of naturalistic everyday situations, extending structured models of action understanding to open-ended contexts. Across six preregistered experiments (N = 1,554), the model captures people's inferences about desires, physical environments, and social relationships. This work formalizes how relationships can constrain -- and be revealed through -- everyday action.
tldr: This paper presents a computational model that formalizes how social relationships, treated as constraints, shape the interpretation of everyday actions in naturalistic scenarios.
motivation: The authors aim to provide a formal account of how structured, shared knowledge about social relationships influences action interpretation, drawing an analogy to physical constraints in generative models.
method: The model represents relationships as constraints within a generative framework of action understanding and is tested in six preregistered experiments (N=1,554) involving naturalistic stories.
result: The model effectively captures human inferences about desires, physical environments, and social relationships across the experiments.
conclusion: The work demonstrates that social relationships can both constrain and be revealed through everyday actions, extending structured models of action understanding to more open-ended social contexts.

title: Bilinear Correlations In Fluctuating Gaussian States With Anti-unitary Symmetries
authors: Xu Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01724v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study bilinear order-parameter correlations in a general class of sign problem-free systems that are described by what we call Fluctuating Gaussian States (FGS) with anti-unitary symmetries, where the weight of each Gaussian measurement in the space-time path integral is positive-definite. Supported by Monte Carlo simulations on fluctuating Gaussian fermionic and bosonic examples, we argue that such systems generally exhibit two types of broken-symmetry phases: a and a , with the competition between the two determined by the stability of the fluctuation saddle point of FGS. Due to the Fermi liquid instability in fermionic FGS with anti-unitary symmetries, we also discuss the possibility of representing fermionic FGS with a particular Projected Entangled-Pair State (PEPS) ansatz, which we argue a certain construction provides an efficient description for the saddle point phase, but not for the non-local contraction phase. Finally, we discuss the potential implication of our result in non-equilibrium systems and stabilizing a target bilinear order.
tldr: The paper analyzes bilinear correlations in fluctuating Gaussian states with anti-unitary symmetries, revealing symmetry-broken phases and discussing PEPS representation.
motivation: To understand symmetry breaking in sign-problem-free many-body systems with anti-unitary symmetries.
method: Uses Monte Carlo simulations on fermionic and bosonic examples, combined with saddle-point analysis and a proposed PEPS ansatz.
result: Identifies two types of broken-symmetry phases determined by fluctuation saddle-point stability, and shows the PEPS description is efficient only for the saddle-point phase.
conclusion: The findings have implications for non-equilibrium systems and stabilizing target bilinear orders.

title: Extended Body Propagators
authors: Rory O'dwyer
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01829v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Three seemingly distinct extended-body propagators devised by Ansoldi et al., Erbin et al., and Stanford et al.\ respectively arise in completely different settings, though each can be considered a realization of the Polyakov path integral. This paper proves that the Ansoldi propagator corresponds to the characteristic function of the random variable with the probability density function [MATH] in ambient dimension [MATH], of scale [MATH]. The exponent is fixed by the dimension and by nothing else in the Ansoldi/geometric comparison; the on-shell two-point amplitude of Erbin et al. and JT gravity agree with its [MATH] member in the senses made precise below. After an extensive literature review, the author believes that this observation and constructed area measure is novel. The area measure will, however, emerge as the natural candidate for the extension of the earlier non-extended body path space measures to two dimensional simplicial complexes. We further show that the area measure of this paper is exactly the law of the area of a triangle, two of whose sides are drawn from the measure obtained in the companion manuscripts for the one-dimensional Polyakov integral. tldr: This paper establishes correspondences between three distinct extended-body propagators and introduces a novel area measure rooted in the Polyakov path integral, with implications for JT gravity.
motivation: The paper aims to unify different formulations of extended-body propagators and to construct a well-defined area measure for path integrals over two-dimensional surfaces.
method: The author proves that the Ansoldi propagator corresponds to a characteristic function, constructs an area measure, and shows its equivalence to the area distribution of a triangle under specific measures.
result: The constructed area measure is shown to be novel and consistent with the on-shell two-point amplitude of Erbin et al. and JT gravity for a specific case, and it serves as a natural extension of non-extended measures to two-dimensional simplicial complexes.
conclusion: The paper provides a rigorous argument reducing the measure of tubular worldsheets to that of a triangle, suggesting a deeper geometric structure underlying these propagators.

title: Applying The Convolution Theorem To The Two-dimensional Magnetic Inverse Problem
authors: Michael T. M. Woodley
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01862v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A collection and clarification is given of the key mathematical details of the method of applying the convolution theorem as part of the solution to the two-dimensional magnetic inverse problem: reconstructing current density from magnetic field data. Particular emphasis is given to obtaining a closed-form solution for the Fourier transform of the convolution kernel that features in the Biot-Savart law. Having done this, the Fourier-transformed current density is obtained, via the convolution theorem, as a function of Fourier-transformed magnetic field data and other variables.
tldr: This paper presents a mathematical method for reconstructing current density from magnetic field data using the convolution theorem.
motivation: To provide a clear derivation of the Fourier transform of the convolution kernel in the Biot-Savart law for two-dimensional magnetic inverse problems.
method: The authors derive a closed-form solution for the Fourier transform of the convolution kernel and apply the convolution theorem to relate Fourier-transformed magnetic field data to current density.
result: A systematic approach to reconstructing current density from magnetic field data is established, with explicit mathematical details.
conclusion: The method offers a rigorous mathematical framework for solving the two-dimensional magnetic inverse problem.

title: Physics-informed Learning For Orbital Uncertainty Propagation With Error Bounds
authors: Chun-Wei Kong, Morteza Lahijanian, Jay Mcmahon
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01881v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Fokker-Planck partial differential equation (FP-PDE) governs uncertainty evolution in stochastic dynamical systems. In orbital dynamics, solving the FP-PDE is challenging because of nonlinear motion, high-dimensional states, and large space-time domains. We develop a physics-informed neural network (PINN) approach that approximates the FP-PDE solution as a single space-time probability density, while also quantifying its worst-case approximation error. This approach is, in principle, independent of the choice of state coordinates and neural network architecture. Specifically, to enforce probability density function (PDF) properties into the neural network, we design a Physics-informed Gaussian mixture model (PINN-GMM). Then a companion error PINN learns the dynamics of the approximation error and yields time-dependent bounds that define an ambiguity set of PDFs. This ambiguity set enables rigorous computation of upper and lower bounds on event probabilities through tractable linear programs. Numerical studies on illustrative 1D examples and several 4D--6D orbital test cases demonstrate accurate uncertainty propagation, correct and informative error bounds, and improved reliability over common uncertainty-propagation baseline methods (Gaussian approximation, unscented transform, and Gaussian mixture model). Constructing the PINN-GMM requires offline training, making it costlier than the baseline approximations; once trained, however, a single forward pass returns the density at any time in sub-millisecond time [MATH] in our implementation).
tldr: This paper develops a physics-informed neural network approach to solve the Fokker-Planck equation for orbital uncertainty propagation, providing error bounds and efficient density estimation.
motivation: Orbital uncertainty propagation is challenging due to nonlinear dynamics and high-dimensional state spaces, and existing methods lack rigorous error quantification.
method: The authors propose a Physics-informed Gaussian mixture model (PINN-GMM) that integrates physical constraints into neural networks to approximate the probability density function, along with a companion error PINN to bound approximation errors and compute event probability bounds via linear programs.
result: Numerical experiments on 1D examples and 4D-6D orbital cases show accurate uncertainty propagation with informative error bounds, outperforming baseline methods like Gaussian approximation and unscented transform, albeit with higher offline training cost.
conclusion: The proposed method offers a novel machine learning-based tool for uncertainty quantification in orbital dynamics, but it is outside the scope of the user's research interests in quantum information.

title: Microscopic Dynamics Of Contagion Using Active Brownian Particles: Universal Scaling And Propagation Controlled By Protection
authors: Francisco Alarc\'on Isela Sicar\'u Regalado-Alvarado
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01927v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding how individual protection and population density influence epidemic spreading remains a central challenge in epidemiology. While classical compartmental models successfully describe the temporal evolution of epidemics, they do not explicitly account for the microscopic motion and spatial organisation of individuals. Here, we investigate contagion dynamics using an agent-based model of Active Brownian Particles (ABPs), where self-propelled agents interact through local contact and a prescribed fraction of the population is protected. By systematically varying the protected-agent fraction and the population density, we identify two distinct contagion regimes separated by a crossover protection of approximately [MATH]. Below this threshold, the maximum contagion rate follows the universal scaling [MATH], indicating that disease transmission is governed primarily by frequency of encounters. Above the threshold, universal scaling is lost and protection becomes the dominant mechanism controlling epidemic spreading, with the strongest suppression occurring in low-density populations. These results demonstrate that microscopic active-matter models provide a powerful framework for investigating epidemic dynamics beyond the assumptions of well-mixed population models and reveal how spatial organisation and individual protection jointly determine contagion dynamics.
tldr: This paper uses active Brownian particles to model epidemic contagion, finding universal scaling of maximum contagion rate below a protection threshold and loss of scaling above it.
motivation: To understand how individual protection and population density influence epidemic spreading beyond well-mixed compartmental models.
method: Agent-based simulations of active Brownian particles with local contact and varying protected fraction and density.
result: Two contagion regimes separated by a crossover protection; below threshold, contagion rate follows universal scaling with density; above, protection dominates.
conclusion: Microscopic active-matter models provide a framework for epidemic dynamics beyond well-mixed assumptions.

title: On The Convergence Of Metadynamics With Gaussian Hills
authors: Olga Rogacheva Andrey Badanin
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01934v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metadynamics is a class of enhanced-sampling methods that is widely used in molecular modeling. Here, we consider metadynamics with a one-dimensional collective variable and explore the limitations of using Gaussian hills in light of existing convergence results. We reduce the corresponding evolution problem to a replicator-type differential equation and analyze its long-time behavior. For a periodic collective variable, we prove the convergence of metadynamics. However, the situation is fundamentally different when the collective variable is defined on a finite interval. In this case, the stationary solution only exists in the weak sense as a finite atomic measure. The solution to the differential equation weakly converges to it. Consequently, metadynamics is ineffective due to the absence of a clear quasi-stationary state. A quasi-stationary, transient solution can only be captured in the "INTERVAL" framework if the free energy outside the finite interval remains nearly constant across sufficiently large regions compared to [MATH].
tldr: This paper analyzes the convergence of metadynamics with Gaussian hills for molecular dynamics, proving convergence for periodic collective variables but showing ineffectiveness on finite intervals due to weak convergence to an atomic measure.
motivation: To understand the limitations of metadynamics when using Gaussian hills, especially when the collective variable is defined on a finite interval, as this affects the reliability of free-energy sampling.
method: The evolution problem is reduced to a replicator-type differential equation, and its long-time behavior is analyzed via weak convergence and measure-theoretic arguments.
result: For periodic collective variables, convergence is proven. For finite intervals, the stationary solution only exists weakly as a finite atomic measure, and the solution weakly converges to it, indicating no clear quasi-stationary state.
conclusion: Metadynamics is ineffective on finite intervals unless the free energy outside the interval is nearly constant over sufficiently large regions, limiting its applicability in such scenarios.

title: Quantum MeanFlow: Single-shot Generative Sampling On Nisq Hardware
authors: Ashish Joshi, Eshaan Mistry, Takahiko Koyama
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02186v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum generative models offer a promising framework for exploring whether quantum computation can enhance generative machine learning. Flow matching is a generative method in which samples are generated by transporting a simple, known distribution to the target data distribution with a learned velocity field. Its quantum counterpart, known as quantum flow matching (QFM), was introduced recently, and, like its classical counterpart, requires integrating an ordinary differential equation over many time steps during inference. As each step requires the output from the previous step, the circuit submission is sequential and a drawback on quantum computers as they have high input/output costs. To alleviate this problem, we introduce Quantum MeanFlow (QMF), the quantum analogue of the MeanFlow formulation, which allows single-step sample generation. While the QFM learns an instantaneous velocity field at each time step, QMF learns the average velocity over a time interval. We use a parameterized quantum circuit to learn these velocity fields and benchmark the two methods on the MNIST dataset. We show that while single-step QMF has lower image quality compared to multi-step QFM, it performs better than the single-step QFM sampling at every shot count. Both of our models are executed on IBM quantum computers and best-of-N rejection sampling recovers most of the accuracy lost to device noise without modifying the circuit. This is especially advantageous for QMF which has only one circuit evaluation per image. Here, We establish QMF as a viable method for single-step quantum generative sampling, saving on quantum circuit evaluations per generated sample.
tldr: Quantum MeanFlow is a single-step quantum generative model that learns an average velocity field to reduce circuit evaluations, demonstrated on IBM quantum computers.
motivation: Quantum flow matching requires multiple sequential steps with high I/O costs; single-step generation would be more efficient on NISQ hardware.
method: QMF learns an average velocity over a time interval using a parameterized quantum circuit, enabling single-shot sampling; it is benchmarked against QFM on MNIST.
result: Single-step QMF yields lower image quality than multi-step QFM but outperforms single-step QFM at every shot count; best-of-N rejection sampling mitigates device noise.
conclusion: QMF is a viable approach for single-step quantum generative sampling, reducing circuit evaluations per sample and improving practicality on current quantum devices.

title: Solomonoff Induction And Singular Integrals
authors: Daniel Murfet Will Troiani
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01666v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Solomonoff distribution [MATH] assigns an a priori probability to a finite binary string [MATH] by summing over all programs whose output begins with [MATH], weighting a program of length [MATH] by [MATH]. Thus, likely strings are those with many short explanations. This appears to be a purely discrete notion of complexity. However, Riemann sums are also countable. conclusion: The work establishes a formal connection between algorithmic information and statistical learning theory, with implications for understanding model selection.

title: BiLipschitz And Bounded Displacement Equivalence Of Delone Sets
authors: Yaar Solomon Smilansky Yotam
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01763v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We survey biLipschitz (BL) and bounded displacement (BD) equivalence of Delone sets, with an emphasis on examples arising in aperiodic order. After recalling the classical results of Burago-Kleiner, McMullen, and Laczkovich, we discuss criteria for rectifiability, uniform spreadness, and BD equivalence, and how these relate to discrepancy and point-counting estimates. We then focus on Delone sets associated with substitution tilings, where these questions can often be studied through the combinatorial and spectral properties of the underlying substitution rules. We also consider selected classes of cut-and-project sets and briefly discuss extensions beyond BL and BD equivalence.
tldr: This survey examines biLipschitz and bounded displacement equivalence of Delone sets in aperiodic order, with emphasis on substitution tilings and cut-and-project sets.
motivation: The paper aims to synthesize classical results and recent developments on geometric equivalence relations among Delone sets, which are fundamental in aperiodic order and tiling theory.
method: The authors review key criteria (rectifiability, uniform spreadness, BD equivalence) and analyze how combinatorial and spectral properties of substitution rules influence these equivalence relations, also touching on cut-and-project sets.
result: The survey consolidates known theorems and highlights the role of substitution dynamics in determining biLipschitz and bounded displacement equivalence, without presenting new experimental or computational findings.
conclusion: This is a pure mathematics survey unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid systems, and thus falls outside the research scope.

title: On Exposed (Symmetric) Tensors
authors: Sheldon Dantas, Martin Mazzitelli, Jorge Tom\'as Rodr\'iguez
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01835v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We provide an example of a projective tensor product whose unit ball contains an exposed tensor which is not elementary. We then transfer the construction to the symmetric projective tensor product and obtain an analogous result in that setting. Finally, we extend both constructions to projective tensor products with an arbitrary number of factors and to symmetric projective tensor products of every degree.
tldr: The paper constructs examples of exposed, but not elementary, tensors in projective tensor products, including symmetric and arbitrary-rank cases.
motivation: To explore the geometric structure of projective tensor product unit balls, specifically whether every exposed tensor must be elementary.
method: Constructs explicit counterexamples in projective tensor products of two spaces, then extends the construction to symmetric projective tensor products and to products with an arbitrary number of factors (and symmetric products of every degree).
result: Provides explicit tensors in both projective and symmetric projective tensor products that are exposed but not elementary, for any finite number of factors or degree.
conclusion: Shows that exposed tensors need not be elementary in these settings, clarifying the relationship between these concepts in the geometry of tensor products.

title: The Order Of The Non-universal Tree Of A Hilbert Space With Respect To The Haar Basis
authors: Sam Whitmire
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01885v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In his 1994 doctoral thesis, Bossard introduced the notion of the non-universal tree [MATH] associated with each separable Banach space [MATH] which does not contain an isomorphic copy of [MATH]. Together with the order operation defined on well-founded trees, we obtain a method of classifying the complexity of separable Banach spaces by the degree of isomorphism of finite-dimensional subspaces of [MATH]. Despite further refinement of this concept in later years, we are unaware of any specific instances of direct exhibitions of the order of the non-universal tree for a concrete space and basis. We show that if [MATH] is any separable Hilbert space, then [MATH] when taken with respect to the Haar basis for [MATH], demonstrating that the class of Hilbert spaces is the least complex class with respect to this measurement when considering this basis.
tldr: This paper proves that for a separable Hilbert space, the non-universal tree with respect to the Haar basis has the minimal possible order, classifying Hilbert spaces as least complex among separable Banach spaces.
motivation: To classify separable Banach spaces by the complexity of their finite-dimensional subspace structure using the non-universal tree and its order.
method: The paper uses concepts from Banach space theory, in particular well-founded trees and the order operation on trees, to analyze the specific case of a Hilbert space with the Haar basis.
result: It shows that the order of the non-universal tree for a Hilbert space with respect to the Haar basis is the smallest possible, indicating that Hilbert spaces are the least complex class under this measurement.
conclusion: This provides a concrete example of the order of the non-universal tree and establishes Hilbert spaces as the least complex class in this framework.

title: On The Integrability Of The Kirchhoff-Pohozaev Equation On Tori
authors: Dario Bambusi, Emanuele Haus, Simone Marrocco, Michela Procesi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01891v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper we study the Kirchhoff-Pohozaev equation introduced in and its constants of motion (see , ) on [MATH] dimensional tori. We show that these Hamiltonians are all in involution and we prove that they are generated by an infinite list of constants of motion which are all defined and in involution on a fixed phase space. Then we study the Kirchhoff-Pohozaev equation restricted to a finite Fourier support. In dimension [MATH] we show that such finite dimensional reduction is always completely integrable and provide an analytic Brikhoff normal form in a neighborhood of the origin. We also give sufficient conditions for integrability for [MATH]. We finally show that the formal Birkhoff Normal form of the Kirchhoff-Pohozaev equation is integrable for [MATH].
