motivation: To understand the integrability properties of a nonlinear wave equation with nonlocal terms on tori, extending prior work on its constants of motion.
method: The authors analyze an infinite set of constants of motion, prove their involution on a fixed phase space, and examine finite-dimensional truncations to derive analytic Birkhoff normal forms near the origin in dimension 1, with sufficient conditions for higher dimensions.
result: For dimension 1, the finite-dimensional reduction is always completely integrable; for higher dimensions, they provide sufficient conditions and show formal Birkhoff normal form integrability for certain cases.
conclusion: The Kirchhoff-Pohozaev equation exhibits a rich integrable structure, with formal integrability holding in some settings, but this is unrelated to the user's research areas in quantum information and thermodynamics.

title: Bounds-Constrained Finite Element Approximation Of Time-Dependent Partial Differential Equations
authors: John D. Stephens Robert C. Kirby
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01915v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Finite elements provide accurate and efficient methods for the numerical solution of partial differential equations by means of restricting variational problems to finite-dimensional approximating spaces. However, they do not, in general, guarantee enforcement of bounds constraints inherent in the original problem. We propose two approaches to enforcing bounds constraints for time-dependent problems. First, we propose general projective methods which result from a systematic modification of any abstract time-stepping scheme. Second, we present a monolithic technique for which we take a modified formulation of implicit single-stage Runge-Kutta methods and general implicit multistep methods as prototypical examples. By solving a constrained optimization problem, we are able to ensure that the bounds constraints are enforced by the approximate solution at the discrete time levels, obtaining (formally) high order methods both in space and time. Numerical examples for the linear heat and advection equations and nonlinear Allen-Cahn equation are given.
tldr: This paper presents methods for enforcing bounds constraints in finite element approximations of time-dependent PDEs.
motivation: Standard finite element methods do not guarantee that numerical solutions respect inherent bounds (e.g., positivity).
method: Two approaches are introduced: projective methods modifying time-stepping schemes, and a monolithic technique using modified implicit Runge-Kutta and multistep methods with constrained optimization.
result: Numerical examples demonstrate that the methods enforce bounds while maintaining high-order accuracy in space and time.
conclusion: The proposed techniques effectively enforce bounds constraints without sacrificing formal accuracy.

title: New Strategies For Some Pursuit-evasion Differential Games With Gronwall-type Constraints
authors: Jamilu Adamu, Mehdi Salimi, Farouq Abba Wabi, Jewaidu Rilwan
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01922v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper studies a class of non-cooperative pursuit-evasion differential games in the sequence space [MATH] The motions of the pursuer and the evader are described by certain first-order differential equations while their control functions are subject to Gronwall-type constraints which impose history-dependent bounds on their control resources. Two fundamental problems are investigated. For the pursuit problem, new strategy for the pursuer is constructed and sufficient conditions guaranteeing the completion of pursuit are established. For evasion problem, an admissible strategy of the evader ensuring avoidance of capture is obtained, and corresponding sufficient conditions for successful evasion are derived. The proposed approached extends existing results on differential games with classical geometric and integral constraints to a broader class of systems governed by Gronwall-type restrictions.
tldr: This paper develops new strategies for pursuit-evasion differential games with Gronwall-type constraints, establishing sufficient conditions for both pursuit completion and evasion success.
motivation: To extend classical differential game theory beyond geometric and integral constraints to history-dependent Gronwall-type bounds, which are more general and practical.
method: Constructs admissible strategies for pursuer and evader in sequence space, and derives sufficient conditions using Gronwall-type inequalities.
result: Provides new sufficient conditions for guaranteed pursuit and successful evasion, generalizing prior work with classical constraints.
conclusion: Demonstrates that pursuit-evasion games with Gronwall-type constraints admit strategies under broad conditions, opening a new class of problems for analysis.

title: On Sum Ranges For $3n$-convergence
authors: Preston Martens
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01926v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Riemann Rearrangement Theorem (RRT) tells us that commutativity of infinite series can differ from finite series. We wish to extend the notion of infinite series rearrangements to weaker forms of convergence, such as partial series convergence on every 2nd or 3rd index, called [MATH]- or [MATH]-convergence. In the case of [MATH]-convergence, it has been shown that the sum range, along with the standard cases in the RRT, can produce a shifted additive subgroup of reals. In this paper, we show cases where the [MATH]-sum range is still a subgroup and a case where the [MATH]-sum range cannot be a subgroup, proving the existence of more depth for [MATH]-convergence.
tldr: This paper extends the Riemann Rearrangement Theorem to weaker forms of convergence, specifically 3n-convergence, and investigates the possible sum ranges.
motivation: To understand how commutativity and rearrangement properties of infinite series behave under weaker convergence notions like 3n-convergence.
method: The author analyzes the sum range for 3n-convergent series, examining cases where the sum range is an additive subgroup and searching for counterexamples.
result: It is shown that in some cases the 3n-sum range remains a subgroup, but a case exists where it cannot be a subgroup, demonstrating additional complexity.
conclusion: The existence of non-subgroup sum ranges for 3n-convergence reveals deeper structure beyond standard Riemann Rearrangement scenarios.

title: Isac With Co-Prime Arrays: Virtual-Aperture Sensing And Uplink Downlink Communications
authors: Jing Zhang, Yuxiao Liu, Jiayi Sun, Junliang Ye, Derrick Wing Kwan Ng
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01979v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) enables simultaneous communication and environmental sensing in unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) networks, but its performance is constrained by the physical antenna aperture and residual self-interference (SI) in full-duplex (FD) sensing. To address these issues, we propose a shared-aperture ISAC architecture in which a sparse co-prime array (CPA) is embedded in a uniform linear array (ULA) grid for FD sensing, while the remaining antenna positions support time-division duplexing (TDD) communication. We characterize the sensing performance through an order-wise Cramer-Rao bound (CRB) analysis, showing that the CPA achieves a stronger asymptotic sensing gain than the partitioned ULA benchmark in both single-target and nondegenerate multi-target scenarios. We further reveal a space-time sampling tradeoff under the same physical aperture. Based on the proposed architecture, we formulate a non-convex joint resource allocation problem that maximizes the weighted downlink-uplink sum rate by jointly designing the sensing transmit covariance, downlink precoder, and uplink receive beamformers under sensing accuracy, BS transmit-power, communication QoS, and residual SI constraints. An alternating-optimization-based algorithm is developed. Simulations demonstrate consistent performance gains over the considered baselines and confirm the complementary benefits of the CPA virtual aperture and sensing covariance optimization.
tldr: The paper proposes a shared-aperture ISAC architecture using co-prime arrays for UAV networks, improving sensing and communication performance.
motivation: To address limitations in ISAC due to physical antenna aperture and residual self-interference in full-duplex sensing.
method: It embeds a sparse co-prime array in a uniform linear array for sensing, while remaining antennas support TDD communication; formulates a non-convex joint resource allocation problem solved via alternating optimization.
result: Order-wise Cramer-Rao bound analysis shows stronger asymptotic sensing gain than a partitioned ULA, and simulations demonstrate consistent performance gains over baselines.
conclusion: The co-prime array architecture and covariance optimization yield complementary benefits for ISAC in UAV networks.

title: Spectral Analysis Of Gram Matrices With Missing At Random Observations: Convergence, Central Limit Theorems, And Applications In Statistical Inference
authors: Huiqin Li, Guangming Pan, Yanqing Yin, Wang Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02024v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Motivated by the statistical inference using the Gram matrix in the context of missing at random observations, this paper investigates the spectral properties of the random matrices [MATH], where [MATH] represents a Hadamard random matrix with entries determined by independent Bernoulli variables [MATH]. Operating within the high-dimensional framework, we establish the convergence of the empirical spectral distribution of [MATH] to a well-defined limiting distribution. In addition, we explore the impact of the missing mechanism on the second-order properties of the spectral distribution of the Gram matrix [MATH]. We establish the central limit theorem for the linear spectral statistics of [MATH], shedding light on their fluctuations. Surprisingly, our analysis reveals that even in the ideal Gaussian distribution scenario, the fluctuations of statistics generated by eigenvalues are influenced by the eigenvectors of the population covariance matrix in the missing-at-random case. This discovery uncovers a remarkable phenomenon that starkly contrasts with the classical case. Subsequently, we demonstrate the practical application of our central limit theorem in hypothesis testing for the population covariance matrix.
tldr: A high-dimensional statistics paper on spectral analysis of Gram matrices with missing at random observations, deriving convergence and central limit theorems for covariance testing.
motivation: To understand spectral properties of sample covariance-type matrices when data is missing at random and to develop statistical inference tools.
method: Uses random matrix theory, analyzing the Hadamard product of a data matrix with a Bernoulli mask to derive limiting empirical spectral distribution and central limit theorem for linear spectral statistics.
result: Establishes convergence and fluctuation results, showing eigenvectors of the population covariance affect fluctuations even in the Gaussian case, contrasting with classical results.
conclusion: Provides a practical application to hypothesis testing for the population covariance matrix under missing data.

title: New Binary Optimal Lcd Codes Using Heuristic Embedding
authors: Haeun Lim, Junmin An, Jon-Lark Kim
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02096v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we investigate the construction of binary optimal LCD codes through short LCD embeddings. For this purpose, we design heuristic frameworks based on a greedy algorithm. We explore the search spaces of LCD embeddings using the fact that an invertible matrix together with an arbitrary matrix yields an LCD embedding. We therefore use elementary row operations on the invertible block and single entry-flips on the arbitrary block as local moves in a greedy algorithm. Using this method, we have found [MATH] optimal new LCD codes with dimensions 7 and 8 for lengths from 55 to 201.
tldr: This paper constructs optimal binary LCD codes using heuristic embedding and greedy algorithms.
motivation: To discover new optimal binary LCD codes for various lengths and dimensions, which are useful in classical coding theory.
method: They design a greedy algorithm that explores LCD embeddings using elementary row operations on an invertible block and entry-flips on an arbitrary block.
result: They found many optimal new LCD codes with dimensions 7 and 8 for lengths 55 to 201.
conclusion: The heuristic embedding approach is effective in finding optimal LCD codes.

title: Instance Optimal Sparse Recovery From Nonlinear Observations: A Unified Framework
authors: Arian Maleki Junren Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02120v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper develops a unified framework for instance optimal sparse recovery from nonlinear observations. The main ingredient is a signal-dependent restricted approximate invertibility condition (RAIC) of some gradient, which leads to the instance optimality of iterative hard thresholding. Under Gaussian designs, we apply the proposed framework to phaseless, one-bit, and ReLU measurements, which correspond to the problems of sparse phase retrieval, one-bit compressed sensing, and sparse ReLU regression, respectively. For sparse phase retrieval, we propose a variant of thresholded amplitude flow and show its instance optimality under [MATH] measurements (up to logarithmic factors), where [MATH] is the sparsity level. To our best knowledge, this is the first instance optimal efficient algorithm for sparse phase retrieval and complements Gao, Wang and Xu (2016) that achieved this via a computationally intractable program. In one-bit compressed sensing, we establish the instance optimality of normalized binary iterative hard thresholding and strengthen the recent result of Matsumoto and Mazumdar (2024). In sparse ReLU regression, it is shown that a slight variant of the algorithm in Soltanolkotabi (2017) is instance optimal. Moreover, [MATH] non-uniform instance optimal guarantees are obtained for these problems. The analysis is built upon a number of high-dimensional concentration bounds, including bounds on restricted eigenvalues and a novel instance-dependent hyperplane tessellation result.
tldr: This paper develops a unified framework for instance optimal sparse recovery from nonlinear observations, covering phase retrieval, one-bit compressed sensing, and ReLU regression.
motivation: To provide efficient algorithms with theoretical guarantees for recovering sparse signals from nonlinear measurements, which is a classical signal processing problem without direct connection to quantum information or thermodynamics.
method: Introduces a signal-dependent restricted approximate invertibility condition (RAIC) and proves instance optimality of iterative hard thresholding under this condition, with applications to Gaussian designs and concentration bounds.
result: Achieves the first instance optimal efficient algorithm for sparse phase retrieval, and strengthens instance optimality results for one-bit compressed sensing and sparse ReLU regression.
conclusion: The framework offers a principled approach to sparse recovery from nonlinear observations, but it lies entirely outside the specified research directions in quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid systems.

title: Stochastic Optimal Control Problem Under Inside Information
authors: Jingtao Shi Yuxin Ye
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02164v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper is concerned with a stochastic optimal control problem under inside information. The control process depends on an [MATH]-measurable random variable [MATH], representing the static inside information, and is adapted to the enlarged filtration generated by the underlying Brownian motion and the random variable [MATH]. Accordingly, the traditional stochastic integral fails to be well-defined in this non-adapted setting; we adopt forward integrals to formulate the stochastic integral terms in the system. By means of the Donsker delta function, the original controlled system is transformed into a [MATH]-parameterized system. We further establish the existence of solutions to forward (SDEs), and prove the uniqueness of solutions via flow transformation techniques. Under a Gaussian assumption on [MATH], we derive both necessary and sufficient optimality conditions for the aforementioned control problem. Subsequently, we formulate the (LQ) optimal control problem under inside information. Through the [MATH]-parameterized transformation, the original problem is converted into an LQ control problem with random coefficients. A numerical example for the LQ case is provided at the end to validate our theoretical findings.
tldr: This paper studies stochastic optimal control with inside information using forward integrals and Donsker delta transformations, deriving optimality conditions and an LQ example.
motivation: The research interests focus on quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, and hybrid systems; this paper is purely in stochastic control and finance, unrelated to those areas.
method: It employs forward integrals to handle non-adapted processes, transforms the system via Donsker delta functions, and establishes solution existence and uniqueness using flow transformations.
result: Under Gaussian assumptions, it provides necessary and sufficient optimality conditions and converts the problem into an LQ control with random coefficients, including a numerical example.
conclusion: The work contributes to stochastic optimal control theory but has no connection to the specified research directions, thus it falls outside the scope of interest.

title: Error Estimate Of The Nonuniform Bdf3-l2 Method For Subdiffusion Equations Via Multiscale Solution Decomposition
authors: Wenlin Qiu, Kexin Li, Yiqun Li, Hao Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02178v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Numerical experiments reported by Quan and Wu [SIAM J Numer Anal 61 (2023) 2106-2132] show that the observed temporal convergence rates of nonuniform L2 methods for subdiffusion models are not consistent with the theoretically predicted order [MATH]. This discrepancy suggests that a more refined analysis is needed and motivates the development of a nonuniform BDF3-L2 method for the subdiffusion equation. To account for the initial solution singularity, we employ the multiscale solution decomposition to decompose the original solution and approximate a smoother unknown variable that satisfies the subdiffusion model with a smoother source term. The resulting formulation, however, involves restrictive high-order boundary conditions on the source term and initial data. To overcome this difficulty, we introduce a spectral truncation technique that requires only slightly stronger regularity of the data and a controllable truncation error. We establish high-order regularity estimates of the solution to the truncated problem and develop a nonuniform BDF3-L2 method for its numerical approximation, based on which we derive a rigorous error estimate of temporal convergence order [MATH]. Numerical experiments are carried out to substantiate the theoretical findings.
tldr: This paper develops a nonuniform BDF3-L2 method for subdiffusion equations with rigorous error estimates using multiscale solution decomposition and spectral truncation.
motivation: Observed temporal convergence rates of nonuniform L2 methods for subdiffusion models are inconsistent with theoretical predictions, motivating the development of a more accurate numerical method.
method: The authors employ multiscale solution decomposition to handle initial solution singularities, introduce a spectral truncation technique to relax boundary condition requirements, and construct a nonuniform BDF3-L2 scheme with detailed error analysis.
result: They establish high-order regularity estimates and derive a rigorous error estimate of temporal convergence order, supported by numerical experiments.
conclusion: The proposed nonuniform BDF3-L2 method achieves the theoretically predicted convergence rates, resolving the discrepancy noted in prior work.

title: Invariant Subspaces For Free Linearizations Of Lipschitz Maps
authors: Cl\'ement Coine, Pedro L. Kaufmann, Colin Petitjean, Sebasti\'an Tapia-Garc\'ia
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02213v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider the invariant subspace problem for operators induced by Lipschitz self-maps on Lipschitz-free spaces. Besides the usual free linearizations [MATH] of basepoint-preserving Lipschitz self-maps, we consider a wider class of operators [MATH] which are naturally defined for arbitrary Lipschitz self-maps. We show, among other results, that every [MATH] admits a non-trivial invariant subspace whenever the underlying metric space contains a compact ball, or has at least two connected components one of which has non-empty interior. We also obtain corresponding positive results for [MATH] under isolated-point, compact-ball and disconnectedness assumptions, and discuss some consequences for linear dynamics.
tldr: This paper studies the invariant subspace problem for operators induced by Lipschitz self-maps on Lipschitz-free spaces, establishing existence of nontrivial invariant subspaces under certain metric-space conditions.
motivation: To advance the classical invariant subspace problem in the context of Lipschitz-free spaces and to understand the structure of operators arising from Lipschitz maps.
method: The authors introduce a wider class of operators naturally defined for arbitrary Lipschitz self-maps and analyze conditions such as compact balls, disconnected components, and isolated points to prove invariant subspace existence.
result: They show that every such operator admits a nontrivial invariant subspace when the underlying metric space has a compact ball or at least two connected components with one having non-empty interior, among other findings.
conclusion: The results provide positive solutions to the invariant subspace problem in these settings and have consequences for linear dynamics.

title: Lyapunov Graphs Of Non-singular Morse-Smale Flows On $s^1 \times S^2$
authors: Fangfang Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02271v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Following B. Yu's work on Lyapunov graphs of non-singular Smale flows on [MATH], we characterize the Lyapunov graphs of non-singular Morse-Smale flows on [MATH] by using filtrating neighborhoods as the local data attached to the vertices. More precisely, we determine which oriented graphs with vertices labeled by filtrating neighborhoods can be realized as such Lyapunov graphs.
tldr: This paper characterizes Lyapunov graphs of non-singular Morse-Smale flows on S^1 × S^2 using filtrating neighborhoods as local data at vertices.
motivation: Following B. Yu's work on Lyapunov graphs of non-singular Smale flows, the goal is to extend this characterization to Morse-Smale flows on the specific manifold S^1 × S^2.
method: The author defines Lyapunov graphs with vertices labeled by filtrating neighborhoods and determines which oriented graphs with such labels can be realized from these flows.
result: A complete characterization is given for which oriented graphs with filtrating-neighborhood labels correspond to Lyapunov graphs of non-singular Morse-Smale flows on S^1 × S^2.
conclusion: The result generalizes known classifications to a broader class of flows on a specific 3-manifold, contributing to the topological classification of Morse-Smale flows.

title: Analytic Rigidity And Symbolic Dynamics For Two-centre Billiards
authors: Susanna Terracini Stefano Baranzini
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02310v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish a sharp rigidity--chaos dichotomy for planar two-centre billiards, motivated by a natural analogue of the Birkhoff--Poritsky conjecture: the only tables integrable at every energy should be ellipses confocal with the two centres. Let [MATH] be a bounded domain with [MATH] boundary containing the segment joining the centres. At every fixed energy [MATH], if [MATH] is not a confocal ellipse, we construct billiard trajectories that shadow the stable and unstable manifolds of the collision--reflection orbit and realise arbitrarily prescribed sequences of sufficiently large winding numbers around the segment. This yields an invariant set semiconjugate to the full shift on a countable alphabet, periodic trajectories with prescribed finite itineraries, and compact invariant subsystems with arbitrarily large topological entropy. If, in addition, [MATH] is real-analytic, every real-analytic function on the fixed-energy phase space [MATH] that is invariant under the billiard map is constant. This establishes the real-analytic form of the two-centre Birkhoff--Poritsky conjecture throughout the non-negative-energy regime.
tldr: This paper proves a rigidity-chaos dichotomy for two-centre billiards, establishing that only confocal ellipses are integrable and that any non-elliptic analytic boundary yields chaotic dynamics and a real-analytic Birkhoff-Poritsky rigidity result.
motivation: The work is motivated by the analogue of the Birkhoff–Poritsky conjecture for two-centre billiards, which asks whether the only integrable tables at every energy are confocal ellipses.
method: The authors construct billiard trajectories that shadow stable/unstable manifolds of collision-reflection orbits, using symbolic dynamics to encode winding sequences and compute topological entropy.
result: For non-elliptic boundaries, they prove the existence of an invariant set semiconjugate to a full shift with infinite topological entropy, and for real-analytic boundaries, they show that any real-analytic invariant function is constant.
conclusion: They establish the real-analytic form of the two-centre Birkhoff–Poritsky conjecture for all non-negative energies, confirming the dichotomy between integrable ellipses and chaotic dynamics.

title: Characterizations And Complexity Of Minimum Forward And Integer Cycle Bases
authors: Niels Lindner Gabor Riccardi
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02317v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The cycle space of a directed graph is generated by a cycle basis, where, in general, cycles are allowed to have both forward and backward arcs. In a forward cycle, all arcs must follow the given direction. Several open questions remain regarding the complexity of the minimum cycle basis problem, in particular the minimum-weight integral cycle basis problem, and the minimum-weight weakly and strictly fundamental forward cycle basis problems. In this paper, we address these open questions. First, we study the existence, structure, and computational complexity of minimum-weight forward cycle bases. We give a complete structural characterization of digraphs that admit weakly fundamental (and hence integral) forward cycle bases. We further provide a characterization when a strongly connected digraph admits a forward fundamental cycle basis, proving that such a basis exists if and only if the set of directed cycles has cardinality equal to the cycle rank; in this case, the basis is unique. Lastly, we show that while minimum-weight forward fundamental cycle bases can be found in polynomial time whenever they exist, the minimum-weight forward weakly fundamental cycle basis problem is APX-hard via an L-reduction from the minimum-weight weakly fundamental cycle basis problem on digraphs with metric weights. Second, we introduce opt-in graphs, i.e., the family of graphs for which minimum cycle bases are integral for any weight function. We show that this family is minor-closed and hence, by the Robertson-Seymour theorem, is characterized by a finite set of forbidden minors, so that the opt-in recognition problem is solvable in polynomial time. Lastly, we present an algorithm to check whether a graph is opt-in, and if not, to identify which of its minors belong to the set of forbidden minors. Applying this algorithm, we show that the complete graph [MATH] is opt-in if and only if [MATH].
tldr: The paper addresses open complexity questions for minimum forward and integer cycle bases in directed graphs, providing structural characterizations and complexity results.
motivation: To resolve open problems regarding the computational complexity of minimum-weight forward cycle basis problems and their integrality properties.
method: The authors give structural characterizations of digraphs admitting forward cycle bases, prove APX-hardness through an L-reduction, and introduce opt-in graphs with a polynomial-time recognition algorithm.
result: They characterize when forward cycle bases exist, show polynomial-time solvability for fundamental cases but APX-hardness for weakly fundamental problems, and prove opt-in graphs are minor-closed.
conclusion: The work settles several open questions and provides algorithmic insights into cycle basis problems on directed graphs.

title: $\mathcal{F}$-Transitivity Of Translation Semigroups On Directed Metric Trees
authors: Xiang Chen, Li Zhang, Zehua Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02342v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the [MATH]-transitivity and topological [MATH]-recurrence of left translation semigroups on weighted [MATH]-spaces over directed metric trees. Motivated by the recent work of Mangino and Vargas-Moreno on hypercyclicity and weak mixing for these semigroups, we investigate the different problem of [MATH]-transitivity, where the entire return-time set is required to belong to a prescribed finitely invariant Furstenberg family. Assuming that the weight is [MATH]-admissible, we obtain necessary and sufficient integral conditions for both rooted and rootless trees, and establish the equivalence between [MATH]-transitivity and topological [MATH]-recurrence. In the rooted case, the criteria depend only on the weights along descendant edges. In the rootless case, an additional ancestor term and a measurable cancellation construction reflect the backward geometry of the tree. Our approach is based on measurable weighted minimization and quantitative estimates over subsets of the edge parameter interval. Examples on homogeneous rooted trees and rootless trees with a free left end show that branching may determine the dynamics, but forward branching alone does not guarantee [MATH]-transitivity in the rootless setting.
tldr: This paper investigates F-transitivity and topological F-recurrence for translation semigroups on directed metric trees, providing integral criteria for weighted Lp spaces.
motivation: The study extends recent hypercyclicity and weak mixing results to a more restrictive notion where return times lie in a prescribed Furstenberg family.
method: The authors employ measurable weighted minimization and quantitative estimates over subsets of the edge parameter interval.
result: They derive necessary and sufficient integral conditions for rooted and rootless trees, and establish the equivalence between F-transitivity and topological F-recurrence.
conclusion: The dynamics depend on branching and tree geometry, but forward branching alone does not ensure F-transitivity in the rootless case.

title: On The Duality Between Feature And Sample Screening
authors: Thu-Le Tran
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02418v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Feature and sample screening reduce the cost of machine learning by eliminating irrelevant features and noninformative samples, respectively. Although recognized as primal-dual counterparts, their relationship remains informal and model-dependent. Viewing screening and duality as transformations of objective functions, we introduce Fenchel-Rockafellar (FR) representations, a class of convex problems encompassing the Lasso and SVM that is closed under both transformations. We then prove that feature and sample screening form an equivariant pair: dualization followed by feature screening is equal to sample screening followed by dualization.
tldr: This paper formalizes the duality between feature and sample screening in convex optimization problems such as Lasso and SVM, showing they form an equivariant pair under Fenchel-Rockafellar duality.
motivation: Feature and sample screening are known as primal-dual counterparts in machine learning, but their relationship is informal and model-dependent. The authors aim to provide a unified framework.
method: They introduce Fenchel-Rockafellar (FR) representations, a class of convex problems closed under both screening and dualization, and prove that dualization followed by feature screening equals sample screening followed by dualization.
result: The proof establishes an equivariance between feature and sample screening operations, unifying the two concepts under convex duality.
conclusion: The paper provides a theoretical foundation for screening methods in convex optimization, though it is not related to quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: A Multiscale Finite Element Method For Reaction-diffusion Eigenproblems Arising From Neutronics
authors: Claude Le Bris, Alb\'eric Lefort, Fr\'ed\'eric Legoll
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02420v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider reaction-diffusion eigenproblems with oscillatory diffusion and reaction coefficients. The reaction coefficient magnitude is large: the corrector equation identified by periodic homogenization involves both the diffusion and the reaction operators. We study the numerical approximation of this problem using the Multiscale Finite Element Method (MsFEM). This now classical method is a finite element type method that performs a Galerkin approximation of the oscillatory problem on a specific, problem dependent, basis set. The basis functions are precomputed in an offline stage. Inspired by homogenization theory and using some filtering ideas, we show how to define these basis functions in order to obtain an efficient method. The comprehensive set of numerical experiments that we present, in periodic and non-periodic cases, for the scalar-valued version of the problem (which is then self-adjoint) and for the vector-valued version of the problem (which is then in general non self-adjoint), demonstrates the performance of the approach. Some theoretical arguments complement the numerical observations.
tldr: This paper presents a multiscale finite element method for reaction-diffusion eigenproblems with oscillatory coefficients, common in neutronics, and demonstrates its efficiency through numerical experiments.
motivation: To efficiently solve eigenproblems with highly oscillatory coefficients, leveraging homogenization theory to construct problem-dependent basis functions.
method: The authors use the Multiscale Finite Element Method (MsFEM) with precomputed basis functions inspired by homogenization and filtering, applied to scalar and vector versions of the problem.
result: Numerical experiments in periodic and non-periodic settings show the method's accuracy and efficiency for both self-adjoint and non-self-adjoint cases.
conclusion: The MsFEM approach, guided by homogenization, is effective for this class of reaction-diffusion eigenproblems, with supporting theoretical arguments.

title: Accelerated Convergence Of A Second-Order Dynamical System And Its Application To Splitting Algorithms For Comonotone Inclusions
authors: Jun Dong Yan Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02479v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper introduces a novel second-order dynamical system driven by a forward-backward splitting operator for solving the structured inclusion [MATH] in a real Hilbert space, where [MATH] is a maximal [MATH]-comonotone operator and [MATH] is a [MATH]-cocoercive operator. The well-posedness of the system is established, and Lyapunov analysis yields accelerated convergence rates of order [MATH] for the velocity and [MATH] for the forward-backward residual, together with weak convergence of the trajectories to [MATH]. Temporal discretization further leads to a class of double inertial Halpern forward-backward splitting algorithms that encompasses the classical forward-backward splitting method and its inertial variants as special cases. Numerical experiments on split feasibility, sparse signal recovery, and image deblurring illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm.
tldr: Introduces a second-order dynamical system and double inertial Halpern splitting algorithms for solving comonotone inclusions in Hilbert spaces.
motivation: To accelerate convergence of splitting algorithms for structured inclusions involving comonotone and cocoercive operators.
method: Establishes well-posedness of the dynamical system and uses Lyapunov analysis to derive convergence rates; discretizes in time to obtain inertial algorithms.
result: Achieves accelerated convergence rates for velocity and residual, and weak convergence of trajectories to a solution.
conclusion: The proposed algorithms generalize classical methods and demonstrate effectiveness on numerical examples like image deblurring.

title: Probability-Maximizing Change Detection: Finite-Window Optimality
authors: Javad Heydari Ali Tajer
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02570v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This paper investigates probability-maximizing sequential change detection, a formulation in which performance is measured by the probability of stopping within an admissible interval of duration [MATH] after a change rather than by the expected detection delay. Earlier work introduced this viewpoint in a Bayesian setting and subsequently formalized it under Lorden- and Pollak-type minimax criteria for the case in which successful detection must occur on the post-change observation, i.e., [MATH]. This paper generalizes this framework in two directions. First, the decision maker is allowed to stop within a prescribed window of [MATH] post-change observations. Second, the monitored process is allowed to experience multiple, non-overlapping transient change episodes with unknown onset times and durations, so that success consists of stopping within the admissible window associated with any one of these episodes. False alarms are controlled through an average run-length constraint. For exact finite-sample analysis, the paper introduces a survival-weighted average success criterion, which represents the probability of successfully detecting a randomly encountered change opportunity conditional on the detector being active at its onset. It is established that this criterion admits an exact representation as the expected Shiryaev--Roberts (TSR) statistic at the stopping time normalized by the average run length, and it characterizes its exactly optimal stopping rule. The optimal procedure has finite memory and aggregates the likelihood-ratio evidence corresponding to all possible change onsets within the most recent window and compares the resulting TSR statistic with a continuation boundary obtained from an optimal-stopping formulation.
tldr: This paper generalizes probability-maximizing sequential change detection to allow stopping within a finite window and handle multiple transient change episodes, proving finite-sample optimality via the Shiryaev-Roberts statistic.
motivation: Traditional change detection often uses expected delay, but here the goal is to maximize the probability of detection within an admissible window, which is more practical for applications with time constraints. The paper extends prior work to cover multiple change episodes and finite windows.
method: The authors introduce a survival-weighted average success criterion, which measures the probability of detecting a randomly encountered change episode conditional on the detector being active. They show this criterion is exactly represented by the normalized Shiryaev-Roberts statistic at the stopping time, and solve an optimal-stopping problem to find the optimal rule.
result: The optimal stopping rule is characterized exactly; it has finite memory, aggregates likelihood-ratio evidence over all possible change onsets within the recent window, and compares the resulting statistic to a continuation boundary from an optimal-stopping formulation.
conclusion: The paper provides a rigorous finite-sample optimal solution for probability-maximizing change detection under a finite-window constraint, with the ability to handle multiple transient episodes.

title: Positivity Loss In Bandlimited Spectral Reproduction On Spheres
authors: Hao-Ning Wu
abstract: ArXiv:2609.02695v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How small can the positivity loss be for an [MATH]-bandlimited spectral operator that exactly reproduces all modes up to degree [MATH]? For spherical polynomial approximation on [MATH], we prove that the smallest possible excess of the uniform operator norm above 1, equivalently the least positivity loss, is of sharp order [MATH] when [MATH]. The lower bound follows from a Fej\'er peak test and a concentration estimate for bandlimited kernels, while a matching upper bound is obtained by correcting a positive Jackson operator with a smooth filter. We illustrate the result in three settings. On the circle, taking [MATH], this determines the sharp order of the generalized-projection constant above 1 and identifies the gap between the [MATH] excess of delayed de la Vall\'ee--Poussin means and the optimal [MATH] order. motivation: To understand the fundamental limits of positivity preservation in operators that exactly reproduce spherical harmonics up to a given degree.
method: Uses Fejér peak test and concentration estimates for lower bounds, and corrects a positive Jackson operator with a smooth filter for matching upper bounds.
result: Establishes the sharp order of positivity loss for such operators, and applies to generalized-projection constants, filtered hyperinterpolation, and maximum principle obstructions.

title: Private Computation Space: Experience With Trusted Multi-Cluster Federated Learning For Agriculture
authors: Shuangyu Lei, Muhammad Salman Abid, Jacob Belding, Sam Mosher, Manushi B. Trivedi, Shivranjani Baruah, Liam Wickes-Do, Andrew Anderson, Braulio Dumba, Alyssa Whitcraft, Ritvik Sahajpal, Sijin Li, Kelly Robbins, Michael Gore, Margaret Frank, Steven Wolf, Liz Jones, Abraham Stroock, Kaitlin Gold, Hakim Weatherspoon
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01667v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Artificial Intelligence has shown to help improve agricultural practices, yet adoption remains limited: 69% of U.S. farmers have privacy concerns with sharing their data, and these concerns must be addressed before adoption is widespread. While Federated Learning has been demonstrated to protect privacy at scale for other sectors, deploying a system for agriculture comes with its own set of challenges; the problem necessitates a system that can protect farmer data and identities while preserving model utility, runs on commodity hardware, and is resilient to fragile rural infrastructure. To address these concerns, we introduce the Private Computation Space (PCS), a deployed, open-source Machine Learning system to provision and process farmer data securely. We design a system tailored to an agricultural setting, with multi-cluster orchestration for reliability in rural areas with asynchronous Federated Learning (FL), Differential Privacy (DP), and Trusted Execution Environments (TEEs), to allow farms to participate in the framework while keeping their data private. We evaluate the system on two deployed workloads: monitoring nitrogen with living plant sensors in NY for six months and predicting evapotranspiration from weather stations in CA for ten months. Our evaluation finds a Dice Similarity Coefficient (DSC) of 0.71 and [MATH] accuracy of 0.84 for the respective workloads, improving the worst single-site model accuracy by 22.4% and 9.1%, respectively, while preserving privacy.
tldr: This paper introduces a multi-cluster federated learning system with differential privacy and trusted execution environments to address farmer privacy concerns in agricultural AI applications.
motivation: Farmers are hesitant to share data due to privacy concerns, limiting AI adoption in agriculture; there is a need for a secure, privacy-preserving system that works on commodity hardware in rural areas.
method: The authors design a Private Computation Space (PCS) with asynchronous federated learning, differential privacy, and trusted execution environments, orchestrated across multiple clusters for reliability, and deploy it for two agricultural workloads: nitrogen monitoring with living plant sensors and evapotranspiration prediction from weather stations.
result: The system achieved a Dice Similarity Coefficient of 0.71 for nitrogen monitoring and 0.84 accuracy for evapotranspiration prediction, improving the worst single-site model accuracy by 22.4% and 9.1% respectively while preserving privacy.
conclusion: The PCS demonstrates a practical, deployed system for privacy-preserving agricultural ML, showing that these techniques can be effective without compromising model utility, and addressing key barriers to adoption.

title: Public-Sharing Labels And Verbatim Field Egress In An MCP-to-A2A Agent Configuration: A Controlled Multi-Model Study
authors: Arpan Kumar Mahapatra
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01693v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Safety properties assessed separately for Model Context Protocol (MCP) tool use and Agent2Agent (A2A) delegation need not describe behavior when one agent uses both. We measure one such behavior in a single controlled MCP-to-A2A configuration: a testbed drives a real-model host across a local MCP and a local A2A leg into an ordered event trace scored by exact deterministic rules (no LLM judge), one restricted decision per trial. In a pre-specified, frozen three-arm design, each of 10 record scenarios appears with a CONFIDENTIAL header, with no header, and with PUBLIC - OK TO SHARE; the six substantive record values are byte-identical across arms, and the outcome is verbatim occurrence of any of them in the outbound message. Four models x 3 arms x 4 repeats give 480 trials; the scenario is the unit of generalization, and we report the 10 scenario-level values (mean, median, sign counts), with no p-values or intervals. The confidential-minus-unlabeled contrast is inconclusive and floor-limited in every model (both arms at or near zero), so it does not show that confidential labels lack a protective effect. Adding PUBLIC - OK TO SHARE is descriptively associated with higher verbatim egress relative to the unlabeled baseline, with strong model dependence: strong and consistent for Claude Sonnet 5 (public-minus-unlabeled mean +0.800, all 10 scenarios; mostly an association with whether Claude relays at all), moderate but floor-limited for one GPT-5.6 tier, small (median 0) for another, and a complete floor for the third. This is an association in one configuration, not a causal or general effect. Code, byte-pinned traces, and the offline analysis pipeline are released as a public artifact.
tldr: This paper studies whether confidentiality labels affect information leakage in an MCP-to-A2A agent configuration, finding that confidential labels show no protective effect while public labels are associated with higher verbatim egress.
motivation: To assess safety properties when agents use both MCP tool use and A2A delegation, as separate safety assessments may not capture combined behaviors.
method: The authors ran a controlled three-arm design with four models, three label conditions (confidential, none, public), and 10 record scenarios, measuring verbatim egress via exact deterministic rules over 480 trials.
result: Confidential labels did not reduce egress (floor-limited), while adding 'public' labels was associated with higher egress, especially for Claude Sonnet 5, but with strong model dependence and no causal claims.
conclusion: The association is configuration-specific and not generalizable; further research is needed to understand label effects in multi-agent systems.

title: On Top-Down And Local Lower Bounds For $\mathrm{AC^0}$ Circuits
authors: Benjamin Rossman G\"ulce Karde\c{s}
abstract: ArXiv:2609.01759v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Classical lower bounds for [MATH] circuits proceed bottom-up by simplifying or approximating gates beginning at the input layer. We introduce a complementary top-down model called the Chopping Game, played by adversaries Spoiler and Duplicator on the sets of [MATH]- and [MATH]-inputs of a Boolean function. In each round, Spoiler keeps at least a [MATH]-fraction of one side, and Duplicator arbitrarily restricts the other; Spoiler seeks to minimize (and Duplicator to maximize) the number of rounds until some coordinate separates the two remaining sets. Every depth-[MATH], fan-in-[MATH] circuit induces a [MATH]-round winning strategy for Spoiler, while Duplicator strategies that survive [MATH] rounds formalize top-down lower-bound arguments. Through the Chopping Game and using the polynomial-approximation method, we first obtain the classical lower bound for depth-[MATH] [MATH] circuits in a top-down fashion. We then consider a [MATH]-local variant of the Chopping Game, which relaxes Spoiler's win condition by requiring a separating coordinate within each Hamming ball of radius [MATH], rather than a single coordinate globally. We put forward a conjecture that the [MATH]-round [MATH]-local Chopping Game for [MATH] requires [MATH] in the regime [MATH].
